summary: English adventurer James Brooke used a private warship and bluffed British backing to make himself Rajah of Sarawak on Borneo in 1841, waging brutal anti-pirate wars and preying on teenage boys; his heirs ruled Sarawak as a family fief until 1946.

evidence.note: James Brooke's 1803 birth to a company judge in India is given
First Anglo-Burmese War service and near-fatal wound; transcript misstates the year
Royalist voyage to Sarawak begins; arrival 1839 starts the main events
Brooke extorts the Sultan of Brunei at gunpoint into naming him governor of Sarawak
Anti-pirate campaign with company troops burns villages, framed as near ethnic cleansing
Long segment on Brooke's predatory attention to boys aged about 14 to 17
Badruddin and Hashim killed in palace attack; Badruddin's gunpowder suicide described
1857 Chinese insurrection and the reprisal massacre of about 1,500 Chinese residents
Charles Brooke's rule, expansion and 1890 pamphlet get their own segment
Japanese occupation and the 1946 cession of Sarawak to Britain end the dynasty
Hosts discuss a recent film portraying Brooke heroically, supporting reaches_present

notes: Title names the family, but most airtime is James Brooke, so he is the sole primary; main_span follows his rule (1839-1868) while covered_span runs to the 1946 cession. Victims of his abuse are described as teenage boys, so child-abuse rather than sexual-abuse. Transcript dates for the Burma war and the Royalist sailing are garbled; historical years used. Badruddin's birth year unknown.
